opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

What I keep coming back to is the intersection of language and decision-making. Even before GPT, during my PhD, I was fascinated by the idea of agents that could use language not just to predict the next word, but to actually *do* things: understand instructions, interact with an environment, and learn from feedback. Some of my early work was on text-based games, where an agent has to read a description of the world, decide what to do, and figure out from the outcome whether it was a good choice. That framing has stayed with me.

When we worked on the first GPT paper, the exciting part was seeing how much general knowledge you could pack into a model just through pretraining on lots of text. But to me that was always a foundation, not the end goal. The question I find most compelling is what happens when you take these models and put them in a loop with the world, where they can reason, plan, take actions, use tools, write and run code, and correct themselves.

So these days I'm most drawn to what we call language agents: how do we build them, how do we evaluate them in realistic settings like real software engineering tasks, and how do we make them reliable enough that people can actually trust them with meaningful work? I also care a lot about the evaluation side. As models get more capable, it gets harder to know what they can really do, and good benchmarks end up shaping where the whole field goes.

What excites me is that we've moved from asking "can a model understand language?" to asking "can a model use language to accomplish goals?" That second question is much richer, and I think we're only at the beginning of it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes interest in language agents and moving from language understanding to goal accomplishment, but does not characterize Narasimhan’s preferred research approach as closing the gap between current AI capabilities and a vision one or two steps ahead.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I keep coming back to is agents, systems that don't just answer a question but actually do things in an environment. Read a page, take an action, see what happened, adjust. That's where language models get really interesting to me, because the moment you put a model in a loop with feedback, you expose everything it doesn't understand yet.

Part of that is probably my background. Before the GPT work I was doing reinforcement learning with text, things like agents playing text-based games, where the only observation you get is a paragraph describing the room you're in. That forced a certain kind of thinking: language isn't just something to model statistically, it's an interface for grounding, for planning, for figuring out what to try next. So when large language models arrived, the natural question for me was never just "how well does it complete text," it was "can this thing operate in the world, and how do we tell?"

That second half, the measuring part, is a big chunk of what my group spends time on. Building environments and benchmarks where you can actually watch a model fail in interpretable ways. Web navigation, software engineering tasks, long-horizon reasoning where one wrong step early on compounds. I find failure cases far more informative than leaderboard numbers. A model that gets ninety percent on something tells you less than carefully looking at the ten percent.

And honestly, the thing that keeps it fun is that the gap between what these models look like they can do and what they reliably do is still enormous. Closing that gap, making agents that are actually dependable rather than impressive in a demo, feels like the real problem for the next several years.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he wants to close the gap between what models appear to do and what they can reliably do. It does not characterize that gap as one between current capabilities and what Narasimhan envisions one or two steps ahead.

Language isn’t just a way to communicate; it can also provide instructions, describe goals, and help us learn from other people’s experiences. The question that interests me is how to turn that information into useful behavior: can a system take something you tell it and apply it in a new situation?
